meta.title: Muscle power and fast-twitch fiber with aging: handoff findings
meta.audience: Adults 50+ with declines in muscle function from aging, disuse, injury or catabolic crisis (acute illness, hospitalization, bed rest, major surgery)
meta.rule: Display only key_numbers with safe_to_display true. Use the exact value strings and populations. Where a number is not safe, use the qualitative wording provided.

headline_takeaways: Muscle power, the ability to produce force quickly, tends to fall earlier and often faster than muscle size, and in many studies faster than strength; how much faster varies by person, sex and test.
After about 65, strength and power tend to fall roughly 1 to 2% a year on average (faster at older ages); muscle size usually changes more slowly.
In older men studied by biopsy, fast-twitch (Type II) fibers are noticeably smaller than in younger men, and loss of motor units is a leading explanation under study.
In an 8-year cohort of 565 adults 65+, about 95% of the decline in relative sit-to-stand power was attributed to lower specific power and about 5% to leg muscle loss: size is only part of the story.

Power is trainable: in a 112-person randomized trial, peak power rose 14 to 15% after 8 to 12 weeks of explosive training (light, moderate or heavy loads) vs 3% in controls. That trial measured power, not falls or independence.
Bed rest or time off your feet can lower leg strength and power within days in older adults; gradual, supervised, progressive movement is the supported way back, with your care team's guidance.
Lower sit-to-stand power is associated with more falls history, mobility limitation and mortality in observational studies; association is not proof that training changes those outcomes.

approved_wording.decline_rate: Muscle strength and power tend to begin declining in midlife and, after about 65, often fall by roughly 1 to 2% a year on average, faster for some people and at older ages. Muscle size usually changes more slowly than strength or power.
approved_wording.power_vs_strength: Power tends to fall earlier and faster than strength, though how much faster varies by person, sex and test.
approved_wording.type_ii: In biopsy studies of older men, fast-twitch (Type II) fibers are often noticeably smaller than in younger men, while slow-twitch (Type I) fibers change less.
approved_wording.rfd: Rapid force production tends to be lower in older adults than in younger adults.
approved_wording.disuse: Muscle strength and power can fall within days of bed rest or immobilization, and regaining them takes time and progressive activity.

two_percent_claim_verdict.verdict: Does not hold as stated. No verified source supports a single ~2%/yr decline starting at 40. Mass, strength and power differ in rate and onset.

by_quantity.muscle_mass: Under 1% per year: cross-sectional median 0.47%/yr men, 0.37%/yr women; longitudinal at 75: 0.64-0.70%/yr women, 0.80-0.98%/yr men (PMID 22934016)
by_quantity.strength: About 14-16% per decade (roughly 1.4-1.6%/yr) in mid-to-late life (initial ages 46-78, n=120; PMID 11320101); 3-4%/yr men and 2.5-3%/yr women at age 75 per review (PMID 22934016)
by_quantity.power: Sit-to-stand power about 1-2%/yr after 65 (PMID 41094174, 39790033); leg extensor power ~3.5%/yr cross-sectional 65-89 (PMID 7825481); significant after 50, not significant 30-50 (PMID 34216098)
by_quantity.onset: Baltimore upper-extremity data: declines beginning by age 40 (PMID 9310077); masters athletes 0.55-1.04%/yr at 35-60 in power events (PMID 39019444); athletes are not the general population

two_percent_claim_verdict.defensible_version: Roughly 1 to 2% a year on average for strength and power after about 65, faster at older ages, with muscle size changing more slowly; onset detectable in midlife (about 40 to 50 in some cohorts).

claims_to_avoid: Rate of force development declines 3-5% per year after 50
Type II fiber loss or decline is '2x faster' (than Type I or than anything)
Muscle power declines '2-3x faster than strength' after 50
'About 2% per year after 40' as a single figure
'18-month accelerated decline spiral' after injury or surgery
'Bone demineralization precedes muscle atrophy by 7-14 days'
Power training reduces falls or improves independence or makes you more independent
Power training builds or shifts fast-twitch fibers specifically (not tested)
Fast-twitch fibers are 'lost' or 'dying' in number (primary evidence conflicts; say 'smaller')
Disuse or bed rest hits Type II fibers or power first or most in older adults (untested)
Chen 2023: 'frailty risk +4.7x' as an outcome of osteosarcopenia
Any 'reverse', 'cure', 'fix', 'frail', 'just age' language or fear copy such as 'before it's too late'
Any individual prediction or diagnosis from a power test; cut-offs are research reference points from European cohorts

rules: Never gate or lock any pillar/category
Motion: ease cubic-bezier(0.16,1,0.3,1); include prefers-reduced-motion fallback

disclaimer: Educational information only; not individualized medical advice and not a diagnosis. Discuss new or modified exercise with an appropriate clinician when health or safety concerns apply, including after a recent fall, hospital stay, injury or surgery.
clinician_safety_note: Ask a clinician or physical therapist before adding fast or heavy resistance work after a recent fall, new or worsening pain, balance concerns, hospitalization, surgery, or a heart, joint, bone or neurologic condition. Seek urgent medical care for chest pain, fainting or severe shortness of breath.
